title: Scientific Wiki Template
text:
This guide outlines the basic steps to set up, configure, and publish your own version of this Scientific Wiki.


First, fork this repository to your own GitHub account.



Forking the template


Once this is done, you will have the base template files in your new repository:



Initial repository files


To enable website hosting, you need to create an empty branch called gh-pages. Then, navigate to your repository settings, go to the GitHub Pages section, and select the gh-pages branch as your build and deployment source:



GitHub Pages setup





The main configuration for the website is handled inside the _quarto.yml file. You can customize this file to change the site’s title, logo, navigation sidebar, and bibliography settings:
website:
  title: "Scientific Wiki Template"
  search: true
  sidebar:
    style: "docked"
    logo: "img/logo/logo.png"
    contents:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: "Home"
      - section: "Topics"
        contents:
        - section: "Examples"
          contents:
          - auto: "doc/Examples/*.qmd"
        - section: "Physics"
          contents:
          - auto: "doc/Physics/*.qmd"
      - href: https://github.com/MKReyesH/ScientificWiki
        text: "GitHub Project"
      - href: about.qmd

bibliography: bib/references.bib
csl: bib/journal-of-cosmology-and-astroparticle-physics.csl
You can manage references by adding .bib files to the bib/ folder. You can also change the citation style by updating the csl file path. Quarto supports many Zotero styles, which can be found at the Zotero Style Repository.



Bibliography files





To add new pages to the wiki, simply create new plain text files (with .qmd extension) inside the doc/ folder. The system will automatically recognize the files and add them to the sidebar. The sidebar reproduces the exact folder structure inside the doc/ folder, so you can create drop-down menus simply by placing files inside sub-folders:



Documentation folder structure


All content files must be plain text file using the .qmd extension and must be written using Quarto Markdown syntax. For a detailed guide on native formatting, please see the Quarto Markdown Guide.
Moreover, anticipating that a lot of scientific content is already written in LaTeX, this template also includes (limited) compatibility for simple LaTeX structures. The commands that are safe to use in the .qmd files are explained in the Allowed LaTeX Syntax Guide. For more complex structures like figures or tables, native Markdown syntax must be used.



Every time you commit changes to your repository, GitHub Actions will automatically take care of the deployment phase. The updated webpage will be built and pushed to the gh-pages branch, going live online in just a few minutes.

title: How to create dynamic tables
text: Standard Markdown tables, as shown in the Quarto Markdown Guide, work well for small static datasets. For larger scientific tables requiring live search, sorting, unit conversions, LaTeX math, or literature references, this template provides a custom dynamic-tables filter that renders interactive Tabulator tables directly from .csv files.

title: How to create dynamic tables
text:
Global Options
Global options are specified as key: value pairs at the top of the block:

src: Path to the input .csv file (required).
searchable: Shows or hides the full-row search bar above the table (true or false, default false).
sortable: Enables or disables sorting across all columns (true or false, default true).
per-page: Sets the initial number of rows per page (default 15, with a selector for 10, 15, 25, and 50 rows). The pagination footer hides automatically whenever the active row count fits within one page.

title: How to create dynamic tables
text:
Column Options
Individual columns are configured with col N:, using a 0-based index (col 0: is the first column, col 1: is the second, and so on). Multiple properties for the same column are separated by commas:

header=...: Replaces the CSV header title. Enclose the title in quotes ("..." or '...') if it contains commas; inline math expressions (such as header=$m$) are also supported when latex or latexnum is active (see below).
number / string: Enforces numeric or alphabetical sorting instead of auto-detection (empty cells always sort to the bottom). Numeric columns automatically format extreme magnitudes (\(\vert{}x\vert{} < 10^{-3}\) or \(\vert{}x\vert{} \ge 10^4\)) in exponential notation.
sortable / unsortable: Overrides the global sortable setting for that column.
latex: Renders any LaTeX math syntax ($ ... $, $$ ... $$, \( ... \), or \[ ... \]) in both the column header and cell text via MathJax or KaTeX.
dropdown: Adds a filter menu in the column header populated with all unique values in that column.

::: {.dynamic-table}
src: data/example-table.csv
searchable: true
per-page: 4
col 0: header="Sector", dropdown
col 1: header="Particle", latex
col 2: header="Mass [GeV]", number
col 3: header="Discovery", unsortable
:::

title: How to create dynamic tables
section: Scientific Units, LaTeX Math Numbers, and INSPIRE-HEP Citations
text:
Scientific Units, LaTeX Math Numbers, and INSPIRE-HEP Citations
Three specialized column tags support physical unit scaling, LaTeX scientific notation, and automated bibliography management:

units(Unit1: factor1, Unit2: factor2, ...): Implies number and adds a unit selector to the column header. The first unit listed is active by default; selecting another unit multiplies every numeric cell in the column by its conversion factor.
latexnum: Implies both number and latex. It displays numeric cells as inline math using the same magnitude thresholds as number. For example, 1.057e-4 displays as \(1.06 \times 10^{-4}\). The formatting updates when the user switches units.
inspire: Implies string and treats cell values as INSPIRE-HEP TeX citation keys (multiple keys in one cell can be separated by commas or semicolons, with or without a leading @). During compilation, the filter fetches the corresponding BibTeX records from INSPIRE-HEP in batches, turns each valid key into a clickable [N] CitationKey link that highlights the target entry on click, and renders a live reference list directly below the table that updates as rows are searched, filtered, or paginated. Each table has its own reference list. Consequently, in you make a citation in the main text [1] they will appear in the page bibliography (end of the page), as usual.

::: {.dynamic-table}
src: data/example-table.csv
searchable: true
per-page: 4
col 0: header="Sector", dropdown
col 1: header="Particle", latex
col 2: header=$m$, latexnum, units(GeV: 1, MeV: 1e3, TeV: 1e-3)
col 3: header="Discovery", inspire, unsortable
:::


References


[1] Neddermeyer S H and Anderson C D 1937 Note
on the Nature of Cosmic Ray Particles Phys. Rev.
51 884–6


[2] Perl M L et al 1975
Evidence for Anomalous Lepton Production in e+ - e-
Annihilation Phys. Rev. Lett. 35
1489–92


[3] Abe F et al 1995 Observation of top quark production in p̄p collisions
Phys. Rev. Lett. 74 2626–31


[4] Arnison G et al
1983 Experimental Observation of Isolated Large Transverse
Energy Electrons with Associated Missing Energy at $\sqrt{s}= 540$ GeV Phys.
Lett. B 122 103–16


[5] Arnison G et al
1983 Experimental Observation of Lepton Pairs of Invariant
Mass Around 95-GeV/c2 at the CERN SPS
Collider Phys. Lett. B 126
398–410


[6] Aad G et al 2012 Observation of a new particle in the search for the
Standard Model Higgs boson with the ATLAS detector at the LHC
Phys. Lett. B 716 1–29


[7] Chatrchyan S et al
2012 Observation of a New Boson at a Mass of 125 GeV with the
CMS Experiment at the LHC Phys. Lett. B
716 30–61

title: About this Wiki
text:
About us

    MKReyesH



Powered By

GitHub Pages: Hosting and deployment infrastructure.
Quarto: Markdown rendering, cross-referencing, and website generation.
Pandoc: Document format translation.
Bootstrap and Bootswatch: CSS support and user interface.
MathJax: Mathematical notation rendering.
Gemini: Help writing the Lua filters.



Contributing
If you would like to contribute to the core template, add new LaTeX translation rules, or fix a bug, do not hesitate to open a Pull Request at the GitHub Repository.

title: How to write a page
text: GitHub Pages transforms plain text files into HTML webpages. In this template, files use the .qmd extension and follow Quarto Markdown syntax. Below are examples of the most commonly used formatting structures.

title: How to write a page
text:
This is a subsection

This is a sub-subsection
To make a section cross-referenceable, append an identifier starting with #sec- to the header. For example, typing ## Mathematical Equations {#sec-maths} allows the section to be referenced anywhere in the document using @sec-maths.

title: How to create dynamic plots
text:
Static figures, as shown in the Quarto Markdown Guide, work well for fixed illustrations. For interactive scientific plots—with pannable and zoomable 2D canvases, rotatable 3D scenes, analytical curves and surfaces, external data overlays, shaded regions, LaTeX math labels, and animated parameter sliders—this template provides a custom dynamic-plots filter powered by Plotly.

Basic 2D Curves and Canvas Options
Dynamic plots use tilde-fenced code blocks so formulas are read literally. A ~~~ {#curve .plot-function} block registers a mathematical curve under a unique ID. A ~~~ {.dynamic-plot} block renders one or more registered curves on a shared interactive canvas.
In .plot-function, top-level bracketed parameters define the curve’s domain:

Explicit functions \(y(x)\): Write x: [min, max] to set the horizontal domain and define y as an expression in x. Explicit 2D curves automatically resample at higher resolution when zooming or panning.
Parametric curves \((x(t), y(t))\): Declare a parameter such as t: [0, 2 * pi] and define both x and y in terms of t.
Expressions and styling: Use explicit multiplication (2 * x), JavaScript powers (x ** 2), and parentheses to negate a power (-(x ** 2)). Math names such as sin, sqrt, pi, and e are available directly. Bounds, slider values, and shading constants use the same math syntax. The browser checks and evaluates these settings when the plot loads.
Curve options: points sets the sample count (integer \(\ge 2\), default 100), label sets the legend title (supports inline LaTeX math and defaults to the curve ID), and color sets the trace color. mode selects lines, markers, or lines+markers (default lines). smooth enables spline interpolation on 2D curves (default true).

The ~~~ {.dynamic-plot} block mounts the canvas and configures axes and layout:

curves: Comma-separated list of curve IDs to plot together (required).
xlabel, ylabel: Axis titles, supporting inline LaTeX math ($ ... $, \( ... \)).
xscale, yscale: Axis scaling (linear or log, default linear).
xrange, yrange: Initial axis bounds [min, max] (min < max; bounds must be strictly positive for log scale). For an explicit 2D function on a logarithmic x-axis, set xrange to control the visible positive interval, especially if the function’s domain includes zero.
width, height: Canvas dimensions in pixels, integer \(\ge 200\) (height defaults to 400; when width is omitted, the canvas adapts to the container width).
legend: Shows or hides the collapsible right-hand legend sidebar (true or false, default true).

~~~ {#wave-sin .plot-function}
x: [0, 8]
y: sin(2 * x) * exp(-0.2 * x)
label: $e^{-0.2x}\sin(2x)$
~~~

~~~ {#circle-param .plot-function}
t: [0, 2 * pi]
x: 4 + 0.8 * cos(t)
y: 0.8 * sin(t)
label: $(x - 4)^2 + y^2 = 0.8^2$
color: crimson
~~~

~~~ {.dynamic-plot}
curves: wave-sin, circle-param
xlabel: $x$
ylabel: $y(x)$
~~~



Interactive Sliders, Helper Variables, and Shaded Regions
To make curves interactive or simplify complex formulas, .plot-function supports two optional multi-line blocks:

vars: Defines intermediate variables (name = expr) evaluated sequentially before x and y. Helper variables cannot shadow domain parameters or sliders.
sliders: Declares interactive UI sliders using one of three domain formats:

Continuous range [min, max]: Uniformly sampled into steps discrete values (default 25).
Integer range [a..b]: Discrete integers \(a, a+1, \dots, b\) (a < b).
Explicit value list [v1, v2, v3, ...]: Three or more specific numeric values.

Each slider entry (name: [...]) may be followed by indented option lines: steps (integer \(\ge 2\) for [min, max] ranges, default 25), label (display title above the slider with optional inline LaTeX math; defaults to the parameter name), and play (true or false, default false, adding an independent Play/Pause button in front of that slider’s row). If multiple curves in the same plot declare sliders with the same name and domain, they automatically share a single synchronized slider. A 2D plot without an explicit yrange expands its automatic y-axis bounds when a new slider combination exceeds them.

In 2D plots, .dynamic-plot supports a shade: block using the same entry-plus-options structure. Each entry is written as lower -> upper, shading from the lower boundary up to the upper boundary (where \(y_{\text{lower}}(x) \le y_{\text{upper}}(x)\)):

lower and upper may each be a curve ID listed in curves, a constant expression (such as 0), or a vertical axis bound (bottom on the left to shade everything below a curve, or top on the right to shade everything above a curve; at least one side must be a curve ID). Shading stops at gaps in either curve. Writing curve1 -> curve1 fills the interior of a closed parametric curve with an uninterrupted outline.
Indented options: xrange: [min, max] (not valid for closed-curve curve1 -> curve1 rules), color, opacity in [0, 1] (default 0.2), and label (adds a toggleable area entry to the legend).

~~~ {#gauss-fixed .plot-function}
x: [-4, 6]
vars:
  z = (x - 0.5) / 1.1
y: exp(-0.5 * z**2)
label: $f_1(x)$
color: #1f77b4
~~~

~~~ {#gauss-moving .plot-function}
x: [-4, 6]
sliders:
  mu: [-1.5, 3.5]
    steps: 35
    label: Mean $\mu$
    play: true
  sigma: [0.6, 1.0, 1.4, 1.8]
    label: Width $\sigma$
vars:
  z = (x - mu) / sigma
y: 0.85 * exp(-0.5 * z**2)
label: $f_2(x)$
color: #ff7f0e
~~~

~~~ {.dynamic-plot}
curves: gauss-fixed, gauss-moving
xlabel: $x$
ylabel: Density
shade:
  gauss-fixed -> gauss-moving
    color: #2ca02c
    opacity: 0.22
    label: Excess $f_2(x) \ge f_1(x)$
~~~



Plotting External Data Files
Unlike .plot-function, a ~~~ {#data .plot-file} block takes its sample points directly from the rows of a .csv (comma-separated) or whitespace/tab-delimited numeric file rather than domain parameters (blank lines and comment lines starting with #, %, or // are ignored automatically):

src: Path to the data file (required). Each data row must have the same number of columns, with a finite number in every field.
skip: Number of leading non-comment header rows to ignore, integer \(\ge 0\) (default 0).
x, y, z: Coordinate expressions (x and y required; z optional for 3D) referencing 0-based columns (c0, c1, c2, …) or dynamic column indexing (c(expr), where the result of expr is rounded to the nearest integer to get the column index).
vars:, sliders:, label, color, mode, smooth: Supported just as in .plot-function, except mode defaults to lines+markers and smooth defaults to false.

A .plot-file trace can be overlaid directly with analytical .plot-function curves on the same canvas:
~~~ {#damped-data .plot-file}
src: data/example-plot-damped.csv
skip: 1
x: c0
y: c1
label: Measured amplitude
mode: markers
color: #ff7f0e
~~~

~~~ {#damped-model .plot-function}
x: [0, 10]
y: exp(-0.35 * x) * cos(2 * x)
label: $e^{-0.35t}\cos(2t)$
color: #1f77b4
~~~

~~~ {.dynamic-plot}
curves: damped-model, damped-data
xlabel: Time $t$ [s]
ylabel: Amplitude $A(t)$ [m]
~~~

Combining an integer slider in sliders: with dynamic column indexing (c(k)) sweeps interactively across columns of a multi-column dataset:
~~~ {#wave-sweep .plot-file}
src: data/example-plot-sweep.csv
sliders:
  k: [1..7]
    label: Time index $k$
    play: true
x: c0
y: c(k)
label: Wave amplitude
smooth: true
~~~

~~~ {.dynamic-plot}
curves: wave-sweep
xlabel: $x$ [m]
ylabel: $\psi(x, t_k)$
~~~



3D Curves and Surfaces
Adding a z expression switches a .plot-function to 3D (all curves in a .dynamic-plot must share the same dimensionality, either all 2D or all 3D):

3D parametric curve: 1 domain parameter with x, y, and z.
3D surface: 2 domain parameters with x, y, and z.
points: Sample resolution per domain axis, integer \(\ge 2\) (defaults to 100 for curves and 40 per axis for surfaces).
zlabel, zscale, zrange: Configure the third axis in .dynamic-plot. The 3D axis titles xlabel, ylabel, and zlabel are plain text and default to x, y, and z.

~~~ {#ripple-surface .plot-function}
x: [-4, 4]
y: [-4, 4]
vars:
  r = hypot(x, y)
z: sin(2 * r) / (1 + 0.4 * r)
points: 45
label: Ripple surface
color: #1f77b4
~~~

~~~ {#spiral-3d .plot-function}
t: [0, 4 * pi]
vars:
  r = 0.28 * t
x: r * cos(t)
y: r * sin(t)
z: 0.25 + 0.12 * t
label: Spiral path
color: #d62728
~~~

~~~ {.dynamic-plot}
curves: ripple-surface, spiral-3d
xlabel: x
ylabel: y
zlabel: z(x, y)
~~~

title: How to use LaTeX syntax
text: In the scientific community, it is very common to have texts, equations, and full documents already written in LaTeX. This implies that one needs to translate such content to the Quarto Markdown syntax explained in the previous guide. However, this template allows for the use of some simple LaTeX syntax (in combination with native syntax), which is converted on the fly to the correct Quarto Markdown format. This document serves as both a guide and a test file for the translation rules. It is written using the supported LaTeX commands to explain exactly how the transformation works.

title: How to use LaTeX syntax
text:
This is a subsection

This is a sub-subsection
Because the script converts this directly into native Markdown, the system automatically generates a reference identifier for it based on the heading’s name (lowercase, using hyphens instead of spaces). This allows you to easily link back to the translated section using standard Markdown linking, such as typing [this section](#sections-and-subsections) to navigate back to this section.
